summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework on legal gender recognition, gender markers, health care and hate-crime law. The sources assembled for the City record no municipal statute of its own on those matters and no city-level enforcement figure.

Activists based in Buenos Aires told the Washington Blade, in reporting published on 10 April 2025, that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers in the city has become more common since the current national government took office, and that harassment and hate speech have risen. The account supplies no incident counts and no dates for individual cases, and no later City-specific instance is documented in these sources.

Emergency decree DNU 61/2025, published in February 2025, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. It prohibits people who have legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts describe the decree as illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention. The sources do not record whether the City has adhered or how its prisons have applied the rule.
tangentialFactors:
At national level the administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists linked these measures to the deterioration they described on 10 April 2025.

Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a rise of 62% year-on-year and a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours, according to Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026. The figure is a national raw count that aggregates sexual orientation with gender identity, gives no population denominator and is not broken down by jurisdiction, so it cannot be read as a per-capita magnitude or as a rate for the City.

Of the crimes recorded for 2025, 32% occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, or 142 cases. Most perpetrators were security personnel or unknown assailants. These are national figures covering calendar year 2025.

Emergency decree DNU 62/2025, also published in February 2025, modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for people under 18. A Federal Court ruled the ban unconstitutional in April 2025 and restored access nationwide.
localsOnly:
Trans people employed in Argentina's public sector under the Trans Labor Quota Law have been dismissed by the current administration; the sources give no figure for dismissals within the City's own administration.

INADI's closure removed the national body through which residents could lodge discrimination complaints. The sources assembled for the City do not document a city-level complaint body or its current operation, and whether the City's local anti-discrimination coverage remains operative is unresolved here.

People detained in the City's prisons fall within the scope of DNU 61/2025 if the City adheres to it. FALGBT and legal experts are challenging the decree in court and the sources record no ruling on it.

Families in the City seeking gender-affirming care for minors were affected by DNU 62/2025 until the April 2025 Federal Court judgment restored access; no City-specific implementation detail is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the City of Buenos Aires has adhered to DNU 61/2025, and how its prisons apply the housing rule for transgender detainees, is not sourced here.

No municipal ordinance text on gender identity, gender markers or discrimination was available in the sources for this jurisdiction; the existence and current scope of a City anti-discrimination instrument is unresolved.

The police-violence account from Buenos Aires activists is dated 10 April 2025 and carries no incident counts, no named cases and no dates for individual events. No later City-specific instance is documented in these sources, and an undocumented present should not be read as an absent risk.

Hate-crime figures available for this record are national, raw, aggregated across sexual orientation and gender identity, and carry no denominator or city breakdown; no City-level count, ranking or per-capita figure is available.

No City-level enforcement record for the gender-identity aggravating circumstance in killings, and no City-specific court ruling on the February 2025 decrees, is documented in these sources.
